newsitem.title: HONG KONG: RUGBY UNION-HORDES INVADE HK FOR LAST "BRITISH" SEVENS.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-HORDES INVADE HK FOR LAST "BRITISH" SEVENS.

text.p: Drizzle and cloud overhung the Rugby World Cup Sevens but failed to dampen spirits on Friday as thousands of fans flocked to watch the last Sevens tournament to be staged in Hong Kong under British rule.
The World Cup Sevens, which incorporates the annual Hong Kong Sevens competition, has drawn rugby fans from around the world to Hong Kong just three months before it becomes part of China.

The territory's legendary logistical skills will be tested to the limit over three days as thousands of fans flood the roads to the Hong Kong Stadium, nestled in a residential valley on Hong Kong island.
Hotels and hostels are bursting at the seams with an estimated 15,000 visitors expected to bring in over HK$100 million (US$12.8 million), spending an average of HK$7,000 each during their visit.
Among them are the top brass of many blue chip companies, as well as annual eccentrics and originals, including the "pieman", a well-fleshed London stockbroker known for his beer and pie consumption.
Bars and nightclubs in the Wanchai red light area and Lan Kwai Fong yuppie nightlife district on Hong Kong Island are rolling out the barrel for an invasion of beer-swilling tourists.
Across the harbour in Tsim Sha Tsui, merchants expect a cash bonanza from tourists seeking bargains in electronics, gemstones and silk for which the territory is famed.

Security at the tournament will be provided by stewards drawn from the ranks of the 1st Battalion of the Black Watch regiment, the British army garrison that will be replaced at the handover by China's People's Liberation Army (PLA).
The territory returns to China at midnight on June 30 after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.

Ironically, the Black Watch and the PLA met on the rugby field this week, when a PLA Sports Institute team wiped the smile off the face of British rugby with a 12-7 victory over their Scottish opponents.
The World Cup Sevens runs from kick-off at 12.30 pm on Friday, until the final at 6 pm on Sunday.
Twenty-four teams are in Hong Kong to compete for the Melrose Cup, named after the Scottish football club credited with inventing the game in 1883.
England are the defending champions, having snatched the trophy from Australia in the inaugural World Cup Sevens in Murrayfield in 1993.
They meet Canada in the first game of the tournament.
